claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the stability of a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
Annealing promotes the nucleation and growth of secondary brittle precipitates in high-entropy alloys.
Secondary brittle precipitates act as crack-initiation sites.
Formation of secondary brittle precipitates diminishes toughness relative to the single-phase baseline.
A homogeneous, single-phase disordered high-entropy alloy microstructure delivers high toughness under demanding conditions.
Annealing or aging can be designed to promote secondary-precipitate formation.
The relevant structural change is an increasing volume fraction of brittle precipitates or ordered intermetallic phases at grain boundaries or within the matrix.
Heat treatment reduces configurational disorder.
Reduced configurational disorder facilitates nucleation of brittle phases.
Brittle precipitates disrupt uniform dislocation motion.
Brittle precipitates serve as stress concentrators.
Disrupted dislocation motion and precipitate-induced stress concentration reduce the alloy's capacity to absorb energy.
Reduced energy-absorption capacity lowers toughness.
Heat-treated samples will show secondary-precipitate formation relative to the as-processed baseline.
Heat-treated samples will exhibit lower fracture toughness or impact energy than the baseline.
The as-processed, homogeneously disordered, single-phase condition has optimal toughness.
The proposed behavior applies to compositions and processing conditions near a threshold of phase stability.
The proposed behavior applies within temperature ranges that promote precipitate formation without complete phase separation.
The thermal parameters governing precipitate onset and extent vary with alloy composition.
The quantitative effect of precipitation on toughness varies with alloy composition.
